narrative:
The law school denied your application because the model estimated a 75% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain, but applicants with a similar profile were expected to fail about three times out of four, and the admissions decision treated that risk as too high.

The strongest influence was your third-year academic decile: at 3, it was below the accepted-student average of about 5.79, and it pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar failure. Your first-year decile was the second most important factor; at 5 versus an accepted average of 6, it also pushed toward failure. Your LSAT score of 41 was above the accepted average of about 37.18, so it was the third most important factor and pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to outweigh the academic concerns.

To improve your position, focus on strengthening your academic record, especially in upper-year coursework, and seek advising on bar-exam preparation and study support. You should also ask admissions whether feedback or an appeal or reapplication process is available, and consider reapplying after showing sustained academic improvement. Your LSAT result is a relative strength, so build on it while addressing the third-year performance that weighed most heavily.
